taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes Leache and Reeder (2002) proposed splitting S. undulatus into several species (east of Mobile Bay keeps the name); Animal Diversity Web still treats S. undulatus broadly, including subspecies now proposed as S. cowlesi, S. tristichus and S. consobrinus.
fieldMarks: Gray, brown or rusty lizard, 9-19 cm total length, with keeled scales.
Males have a blue patch on the belly and throat; colour varies geographically.
Northern populations (New York to Maryland) are generally smaller than southern ones.
behavior: Diurnal, active roughly 0600-2000 h; basks on fences, logs, rocks, wood piles and tree trunks, using trunks and branches more in summer.
Males head-bob, do push-ups and flash the blue belly patches to signal territory; territories are roughly 47-61 square metres.
Eats mostly insects, spiders, centipedes and occasionally snails; inactive in cold periods and the hottest part of summer days.
habitat: Mostly arboreal in wooded landscapes in open, sunny situations; also grasslands, shrublands and the edges of pine or hardwood forests.
range: Eastern United States (NatureServe: Alabama, Delaware, DC, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Maryland, Mississippi, North Carolina, New Jersey, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia, West Virginia); Animal Diversity Web gives the broader concept as mid New York to mid Florida and west to Colorado; not in Canada.
